# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. I just watched Heat, Thief, & Collateral for the first time in a back-to-back marathon. I need more movies like this, please!

**Score:** 51
**Body:** Fucking hell. What an experience. I cannot believe that I've never seen these beautiful works of art. Mann is a true master of filming cityscapes at night. I was enthralled the entire time & couldn't take my eyes from the screen.

The score for Thief in particular was mesmerizing. The visceral sound of Heat was unlike anything I've experienced. I watched it with surround sound & those gunshots felt like they were going off right next to me. And I'm still not over the ending of Collateral, Cruise gave one of his best performances.

I definitely need more movie suggestions that fit this vibe. If anyone has anything that hits these notes, please let me know! Thanks for any replies. 🫡 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. to live and die in LA
2. The Town and Hell or High Water.
3. Sicario 1 & 2

P.S. The score for Thief is by Tangerine Dream. Check out their albums!
4. Black Rain 
5. Nightcrawler
6. Ronin
7. Sorcerer (1977) if you loved the score to Thief 
8. Hell yeah. 

Obvious answer would be more Mann, of course. Those 3 are my favorites but Mohicans is very good, Blackhat has good scenes but an incomprehensible plot, and Miami Vice is pretty to look at and has good action, but takes itself way too seriously and also has an absurd plot. The Insider is great but not an action movie. And Manhunter is awesome. I liked it better than Silence of the Lambs. 

I loved Drive. It’s definitely influenced by Thief. 

No Country for Old Men if you haven’t seen it. Fargo is a great crime movie though it’s not as action-driven.

Ronin! Another DeNiro action heist thriller from the 1990s and has one of the greatest car chases ever. 

To Live and Die in LA. - Beautifully shot 1980s action thriller with Willem DaFoe as a compelling villain. 
  - William Petersen double feature - to live and die in LA and Manhunter. 
9. Way of the Gun

## 2. Looking for films that will melt my mind

**Score:** 49
**Body:** I just watched Mulholland drive for the first time and it left me in shock for 20 minutes after. I’m looking for movies that will have a similar effect on me, whether that’s a big twist or just a crazy film.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Lost Highway 
2. Being John Malkovich
3. Pi (1998)
4. Here's a few to get you started: 

Blue Velvet by David Lynch

Memento by Christopher Nolan

Slacker by Richard Linklater

A Clockwork Orange by Stanley Kubrick

Videodrome and Naked Lunch by David Cronenberg 

Repo Man by Alex Cox

Run Lola Run by Tom Tykwer

Naked by Mike Leigh

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind by Michel Gondry

My Own Private Idaho and Drugstore Cowboy by Gus Van Sant

Mystery Train and Night On Earth by Jim Jarmusch
5. Primer 
6. Try Existenz
7. Jacob’s Ladder (1990)

Berberian Sound Studio (2012)
8. Sticking with Lynch, have you seen Eraserhead yet?
9. -Donnie Darko. 

And for something completely different:
-Perfect Days (2023).  Your mind will melt into a warm pleasently gooey pile. You will wonder what you just watched, and how it could make you feel so good. And Calm. And joyful all at the same time. 
10. The Skin I Live In. Will leave you in shock as well. 

## 3. Movies that heavily reference other movies, total pastiche

**Score:** 39
**Body:** By reference I don't mean Deadpool style pop culture references in dialogue. More like Kill Bill, which you could probably reconstruct from thirty other films shot for shot. 

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie 
2. Star Wars - from:

The Hidden Fortress (1958)

The Dam Busters (1955) - the final attack on the Death Star
3. Parody movies like Airplane, Hot Shots, or Scary Movie. 
  - Airplane! is almost a shot-for-shot remake anyway.
4. David Lunch's Wild at Heart.   (Wizard of Oz)
  - David Lunch. 🙂
    - David Lunch the director of Mullholand Drive-Thru
5. Avatar completely stole the plot of the animated movie Fern Gully
  - And Dances With Wolves and Pocahontas
6. The End of Oak Street is definitely modeled on Jaws and BTTF.

## 4. Requesting: happy Anne Hathaway movies

**Score:** 23
**Body:** Fairly recently I've seen three movies of hers (The Odyssey, Interstellar, and Les Mis) and she's great in all of them, but her characters in all three are completely miserable lol

Is there anything more light-hearted or comedic where she plays a substantial or lead role?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Intern
  - One of my favorite comfort movies
2. The Princess Diaries ✨
3. Ocean's Eight - I know this one isn't everyone's cup of tea, but I personally love it. Give me more heist movies with all women casts. 
4. Get Smart
5. Ella Enchanted 
6. Devil Wears Prada
7. Princess Diaries and The Devil Wears Prada are both pretty iconic movie franchises for Anne. Both extremely fun and whimsical.

Also check out Valentine’s Day. It’s more of an ensemble cast, but super lighthearted.
8. Go see End of Oak Street!! It's a ton of fun
9. Lol SUPER light hearted and quite silly but Bride Wars! 

## 5. The Red Shoes (1948)

**Score:** 22
**Body:** If you want to see something that feels truly cinematic, and utilizes incredible editing, filming, production design, music, and dance, you simply must watch this British classic about a ballet company adapting the Hans Christian Andersen tale of the same name.

Not only does this movie feel modern, despite being 80 years old, but the technicolor film processing makes all the colors look absolutely amazing. The ballet sequences use film techniques to transform dancers and sets into something that’s only suggested at by a live dance performance. Furthermore, while many big, song-and-dance movies from Hollywood’s golden era are extremely romantic and optimistic, this movie has a darker side, exploring pursuit of art at all costs, jealousy, and self doubt. 

It’s a fantastic film! 

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Such an amazing movie!! Can't recommend this one enough. 
2. To quote Val (A Chorus Line). “I never heard about the red shoes, I never saw the red shoes, I didn’t give a crap about the red shoes”.

Well, I saw the red shoes. Val missed out, that’s all I am saying.

The fact that I, a straight guy, even know who Val is in A Chorus Line though probably speaks volumes

## 5. Does Ralph Fiennes' The Return have a stronger dialogue and better characters than The Odyssey?

**Score:** 285

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Amazing adaptation. 
  - Both adaptations are great in their own way.

The Return just focuses on a small part of the original poem, which gives the film makers time to work with the characters.  Plus Ralph Fiennes is just an incredible actor.

The Odyssey tries to tell the whole of the original poem - and with a story that has so much going on, they have less time for character development & have to make significant changes to get it to all work within 3 hours.

2. Ooh I forgot about this film. Did you see it? It looked really good. I'm a big fan of Ralph.

3. I didn't get the impression that the dialogue was the top priority in The Odyssey. For all its pretension it was a blockbuster action flick. I'd bet The Odyssey's marketing spend was twice the total budget of The Return.

5. Nolan is total shit at writing dialogue.  "Our age of Bronze..."  ugh. We call it the bronze age, they didn't. And yes, I understood the larger message, that doesn't mean the dialogue isn't bad. 
  - “Stop eating the lotus flower”  
“But I love it”
  - I agree. Movies in which he solely was the dialogue writer don’t have any memorable dialogues. Co-written dialogues with his brother and Goyer have always been better.
    - One addendum I’d make is Inception. The dialogue in that film is written with the same modernist approach as the setting, editing, and construction as the rest of the film, with a sort of hyper intense density. For a film about the methodology of architecture, the dialogue is perfectly suited.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I don't understand the Heaven's Gate reappraisal

**Score:** 94
**Body:** I agree with the sentiment: a film was trashed on release, its director's reputation destroyed and the studio bankrupted based on bad pre-release press and a truncated cut made at the studio's demand. It's exactly the kind of film one wants to reclaim. I just can't see what everyone else sees when they call it a misunderstood masterpiece. I've seen the film twice, both times in the restored 3 1/2-hour version, and both times it's struck me as barely functional from a narrative standpoint, with baffling lapses, longueurs and dog-ends (what's going on with the John Hurt character, to pick just one example?). I also think the filmmaking is a mixed bag: the visuals and production design are both incredible, but Cimino doesn't seem to have a clue what to do with the dialogue scenes, which are all glacial and stilted (except when they feature Sam Waterston, who's giving the best performance in the film and manages to wrest it into something gripping when he's onscreen). And if you ask me, there's something kind of smug and simplistic in the film's misery and "everything sucks" cynicism - the film came at the end of a decade of other films saying similar things, but they don't have the tang of adolescent posturing that this does.

I'm not trying to be combative; I'm just giving my own response to the film. I've tried to like it, but I just can't. To the people who do like it: what am I missing?

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. My favourite trivia about John Hurt is that they left him with nothing to do on set for literally months, so he flew off to go make Elephant Man without telling anyone, came back, and Michael Cimino was none the wiser
  - There are so many great stories about the making of the film. Like how Cimino ordered a street to be pulled down and rebuilt because it looked wrong, despite it having been built to his own specifications in the first place.
    - I do think we've lost something with directors not being coked out anymore 
      - This is the thesis of Megalopolis  
      - Well yeah, instead of crazy stories about wildly wasteful spending on extravagant impulses and artistic whiles, they're now all just "and the studio heads got even more rich".
    - One thing to keep in mind about Cimino is that I get the sense he didn't really want to direct films. He desired to be an architect first, and I think in some ways his films are an expression of that wish fulfillment. There's more to films than just narrative and acting. And a lack of those things shouldn't necessarily be treated as a detriment.

What attracts me to Cimino is the same thing that attracts me to David Lynch, Matthew Barney, Julian Schnabel, Tom Ford, and to some degree Abel Ferrara (he's a filmmaker first, but his films have this same quality).

All of these artists made films that if you're not looking to delve deeper, it would be easy to say "Do these guys even know how to make films?". At least, the structure of their films are not indoctrinated into any filmmaking school.

You can take a scene from several and say this is bad form, this is not how you do this, etc. That's why I enjoy them, they break all kinds of filmmaking rules.

I love when people who don't normally make films (or people who consider themselves artists first) do it, because the result are so different than someone who's studied filmmaking. They are subjectively great to me. Norman Mailer's Tough Guys Don't Dance would never be the beautiful disaster it is without his literary brain struggling to translate what he does on a page to the screen.

Now, back to Heaven's Gate - What I think you need to ask is not why Heaven's Gate doesn't work, but why does the Deer Hunter work? It has many of same problems you mentioned, but the subject matter was so early and so sensitive and Cimino stumbled upon a topic/passion that wasn't siloed, it was collectively on everyone's minds at the time, the Vietnam Elephant in the room, only 3 years after the Fall of Saigon. Cimino cracked that open and then we saw a flood of Vietnam movies for 15+ years where almost any Vietnam movie was elevated in status.

Contrast with Heaven's Gate, where is the audience for the Johnson County War? Same with Year of the Dragon. Although I remember that one at least getting some reception and a lot of cable TV play. Those three films - The Deer Hunter (1978), Heaven's Gate (1980), Year of The Dragon (1985) - are very similarly structured stylistically for Cimino, just against different subjects that fascinated him.

In general, I love his films, but even I have a hard time watching Year of the Dragon because I'm just not that fascinated with what he's trying to show me.

Heaven's Gate was the first Isabelle Huppert film I saw and I still love her in this, even though she's had better performances. I think the leads are a bit wooden. I love the longer version because the cinematography is so brilliant, but you [might enjoy Soderbergh's recut](https://extension765.com/blogs/soderblog/heavens-gate-the-butchers-cut), although he cuts out their school days, which is one section I believe makes the film better. Edit: *apologies, that's not true, he cuts it down and moves it to the end to emphasize the next point as a conclusion.*

These men become learned scholars together, separate, and go make their mark on the world in opposing ways, falling into cynicism and dogma and another upholding idealism in a cold world, I think there's a message there. How do these men come together to learn only to leave and war against each other?

I'll be back in bit with a link.

Edit:

[Michael Cimino interview](https://filmmakermagazine.com/99041-interview-michael-cimino-2005/#.Y_BXTuRMEWM)

Some quotes -

*Cimino: You know, I never studied cinema. I never knew how to make a film, and I still don’t know.*

*I’m quite astonished that I made what I made (laughter). Because, as you must know, my background is architecture, painting, that’s where I come from. I’m much more intrigued by a good building than by a good movie. I’m much more interested in a big bridge or a great new novel or a great painting. When I’m asked about my influences, instead of rolling out 20 filmmakers, I say Frank Lloyd Wright, Degas… Mahler… “Who?” But you have to remember I didn’t come from the film world, I didn’t study film. I once tried to read a book on film editing – after I’d begun doing it! – and I couldn’t finish it, even though it was written by someone who knew a lot about it, I think it was Karel Reisz. And I found it so confusing I had to stop reading it (laughs).*
      - There is a great interview with, of all people, Christopher Lambert, who explains what was Cimino’s problem. Cimino was great at a lot of stuff. He could write, paint, sculpt, direct, etc. According to Lambert, he was the most talented director from the New Hollywood generation. He knew many positions better than the people from the crew. One thing that Cimino couldn’t do was delegating. The problem is that it is a necessity on a film set, where you can’t do everything on your own. And it made him paranoid. 
2. Its reputation has long suggested that it's the worst movie ever made and a total abomination. On watching it, it's hard not to notice that it looks quite beautiful, it's audacious, and it has at least *something* to say. It's a deeply flawed movie and no, it's not a great one by any means, but it's a very interesting failure in a lot of ways. The costumes, the big set pieces etc. I think that's where the reappraisal kicks in. People expecting an abysmal mess and getting a curious failure instead. 

People calling it a lost classic are going too far because it's always cool to be contrarian. But like David Lynch's 'Dune' I defend it as a noble disaster.
3. My dad was actually at said press screening before the sale of United Artists took place. He said that at the films conclusion, there was quite the standing ovation and the next morning many of those clapping, "trashed" the film in their written reviews and thus the sale of the studio took place. I believe from that point on the film was cut significantly and retired to..."The Johnson County Range Wars" or something similar? I think the film, much like Leone's Once Upon a Time in America is a flawed masterpiece, but to each their own.
4. Well, it’s not a conventional American movie, so the screenplay’s narrative isn’t exactly the most important thing. The film’s strength—at least for me—lies in the staging: the way Cimino captures the imagery, the shot composition, the stunning sequences—all of that makes a huge impact on me. The film has an aura of perfection; I don't think I can quite put it into words. 

It possesses a specific kind of formalism that is uncommon in American cinema—a film that seems to seek expression through form rather than necessarily through the text or traditional storytelling. It reminds me of directors like Luchino Visconti, Manoel de Oliveira, or even Raúl Ruiz and Straub & Huillet—filmmakers whose work can be a rather frustrating experience if you watch it with the sole intention of following a story and understanding everything.

## 2. Tree of Life - Did Jessica Chastain got to heaven and the rest didn't?

**Score:** 1
**Body:** I wonder that. Becuase you can see them all in that afterlife beach, but she's the only one getting dresses wonderfully, taken care by multiple angels and is seen alone in that great shot where she is in that flat place?

  
Or maybe they all went to heaven but she got a more special treatment because she was faithful and loyal to God?

  
What are your thoughts on this?

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Luckily, Malick is not such a shitty director that he would end his film with a scoreboard for a sprint to heaven. Even assuming that you see figurative  "heaven" in his films and not, for instance, simply an expression of faith, is kind of pushing it thin. 
2. I took it as her character arriving in heaven first, possibly even later in life and waiting for them to join, but more than that I think you can take whatever meaning you want from it, Malick tends to leave a tiny margin for interpretation 
  - She was there, Pitt's character in hell and the kids purgatory

## 3. Why the recent fixation on something traumatic in the protagonists past?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I say "recent" pretty broadly, like in the last ten or twenty years or so. I've noticed is that a lot of horror/thriller defaults to being centered around some sort of traumatic event in the protagonist past, an event consistently hinted at throughout and finally shown in flashback. The first time I remember seeing it was in Peter Jacksons BRAINDEAD (1992) but back then, it wasn't as overused. On the other hand, there were also Gremlins (1984) which played it for laugh, suggesting that it was a bit old back them.

Personally I'm a bit tired of the trope. What is the appeal? Why did it gain such popularity?

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Cinema has relied on this trope for a lot longer than you think. Some classic horrors which feature a protagonist or villain with a traumatic past include Peeping Tom (1960), Psycho (1960), The Haunting (1963), Don't Look Now (1973) and Halloween (1979). I'm sure there are many more. 

I think it probably comes down at least partly to the love affair between screenwriters and the theories of Sigmund Freud. He was in vogue especially in the 1940s when a lot of Hollywood narrative cinematic language was developing into what it still is now. The idea that a person's present anxieties are linked to something in their past - particularly in their childhood - is one of the core principals of Freudianism.
  - The level and degree and usage percentage of this "trope" hasn't been stagnant over the last century.

I look at communications. Just because there was the printing press, telegraph, telephone, radio, and television, it shouldn't negate the evident leap that came with the Internet and the "smartphone."

Psychology, as you noted, is a huge part of why previous character trauma is stated on the surface level of a story. Bernays, Freud's cousin, wrote books on PR and Propaganda. Goebbels studied Bernays and Freud, and the Nazis provided the roadmap for the advertising world that exploded after WWII. The industry of psychology has grown dramatically since the 1940s, and so has marketing. It could be said that marketing is the style of story that uses psychology to manipulate its audience.

I don't think you were negating anything. I simply wanted to springboard off your quality comment to add to the overall discussion.
2. I’ll take a stab at this. It’s relatively recent in human history. For a long time literature wasn’t based on psychological realism like we are used to. A character acted because of fate. Because of the gods. Because they had a fatal flaw. Nobody knows why hamlet needs to avenge his father from like a personal realistic angle. There’s not scene where hamlet is like “no but I was just closer to my dad cuz he took me to jousting fights and taught me how to wrestle”. It’s a given that a prince avenges his father!   
Then acting teachers like Stella adler and Lee Strasberg and writers like Arthur Miller and Tennessee Williams began a more realistic version of theater and Hollywood caught on and soon you have films where a characters motivation has to be grounded in something real. Generations of writers and actors have now come and gone using that as the rubric.   
That being said, plenty of crappy movies do it sloppily. But take Casablanca from 80+ years ago (Rick is bitter because he lost his true love but through the course of the film starts to see the bigger picture once that love is rekindled) or more recently Anora (Ani wants a better life because her current one is hard). 
3. This has been driving me crazy and really hurting a lot of movies and TV shows for me. There's absolutely no need for it in almost every case. It's like the filmmakers think they need some sort of "reason" for a character to be a certain way, or they need some sort of catalyst event. Like oh no, we can't just have some normal family move into a haunted house, we have to say that one of their kids died or something. 

When you watch 99% of older horror movies they usually just have characters that are like...having a normal time in their life, and then that gets disrupted, you know?
4. It comes out of the realm of marketing, and it's exploded in the last couple decades.

[Here's a New Yorker article](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2022/01/03/the-case-against-the-trauma-plot) that talks about it.

Personally, I find it to be poor, cheap writing. Explaining everything to the audience is bad enough. Adding and addressing backstory trauma to simplify a character's behavior and drives degrades the craft and art of storytelling.
  - No clue why I saw you had a downvote. Your comment is accurate and insightful. I feel like writers use this as a cheating shortcut to make their film feel heavier than it is. 

Like just have someone existing and then build a story around them. I swear it's like 50/50 any new movie we watch, the first scene is a funeral.
    - There's a significant percentage of people who don't like knowing or realizing that their tastes are directly caused by them being manipulated and tricked. It's not merely denial. It's chosen denial. 

It's why people buy things that harm them or that they don't need. It's why people vote against their own self-interests or support candidates that contradict their moral or simply stated codes.

The guilt and shame and feeling of foolishness is what causes people to reject facts and truth that reveal they've been duped. The one fortunate thing for people to know is that marketing works on them regardless of their level of intelligence, so there's no need to feel bad about falling for it. 

But, in the end, people who choose denial are active participants. It's one thing not to see or have come across over a century of people talking about the dangers of marketing, but it's another to reject it and try to shout it out of existence.

Me and my wife notice trends in film/tv a lot and once something starts happening over and over I kind of back off.
